analysis: The supplied units are base-side excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (base lines 36362-37888): token_id arrays, a long_prompt vector with repeated 'cache' content, prompt_contract_id, block_boundaries, chain_hash values and a fixed prompt date. The file is a test fixture holding public golden vectors and contains no secrets, keys, credentials or executable code. The patch excerpt (truncated) shows head-side changes: an added additional_context {enable_thinking:false} member, changed prompt_token_count, chain hashes and token IDs, and removal of a block boundary in some vectors. Those changes regenerate prompt-contract vectors, which suggests a contract change in the prompt rendering/template, such as thinking-disabled handling. The effect on the prefix-cache identity (T-041) and cross-tenant cache keying depends on the unseen provider/coordinator code that consumes this fixture. The base excerpt lines I examined are unchanged context and not in the changed ranges, so no direct finding can cite them. Nothing in the visible fixture data weakens TB-002, TB-011 or the attestation or authorization controls; the fixtures do not alter authorization, encryption or data-exposure behavior. Remaining integration questions: (1) whether the Swift/Go code implementing the new additional_context field and token/chain-hash computation is included in the PR and still binds the scope_id and prompt_contract_id into the cache key, so no cross-tenant sharing is introduced; (2) whether the enable_thinking:false flag is applied identically on the coordinator and provider sides to avoid contract mismatches. This is not a security regression based on the evidence supplied, only an unverified contract between the fixtures and the code; a test-only fixture change is low risk.
